query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing an additional laser remelting pass immediately after each deposited layer during additive manufacturing of high-entropy alloys will improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity by reducing common defects such as porosity and lack-of-fusion.
generation.material_initial_state: Components produced via conventional selective laser melting of high-entropy alloys using standard parameters, typically exhibiting layer-related defects (e.g., porosity, non-uniform microstructure) and slight dimensional inaccuracies.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled, lower-energy laser remelting scan immediately after deposition of each layer to re-melt the top surface.
generation.conditions: The process should be conducted using a selective laser melting system in an inert atmosphere with identical powder feedstock. Both the standard process and the remelt intervention are executed under comparable energy densities and scan speeds, with the only difference being the additional remelt pass on each layer.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined melt pool geometry leading to enhanced metallurgical bonding, reduced porosity, and a more homogenous microstructure with finer grains.
generation.mechanism: The additional laser remelting pass re-melts surface irregularities and partially unmelted regions, promotes full melting and coalescence between layers, relieves residual thermal stresses, and refines the grain structure. This leads to a reduction in fabrication-induced defects and enables higher dimensional accuracy and mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: The remelted components will show lower dimensional deviations and improved mechanical properties—such as higher tensile strength and hardness—relative to components fabricated via the standard AM process.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy components produced by standard AM (selective laser melting) without an additional remelting step.
generation.boundary: Improvements should be observed for process conditions where the remelting pass is properly calibrated; however, if the parameters (e.g., energy density or scan speed) are too aggressive, the benefits may be offset by increased thermal stresses or unwanted microstructural changes.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of mechanical property enhancement and dimensional accuracy improvement may vary with the specific alloy composition and processing conditions, and the balance between reduced defects and potential thermal overstressing needs experimental verification.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of high-entropy alloy components using selective laser melting: one set using the conventional process, and the other set employing an additional laser remelting pass after each layer. Ensure all other process parameters (e.g., laser power, scan speed, powder feedstock, atmosphere) remain constant. Assess and compare the dimensional precision (using high-resolution metrology and CT scanning) and mechanical integrity (via tensile and hardness tests) of both sets.
measurements: Porosity and defect density evaluation (via CT scanning or microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the components produced with the additional remelting pass do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in defects and improvement in both dimensional precision and mechanical properties compared to the standard process samples, or if mechanical integrity deteriorates, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Given the tight coupling between thermal histories, thermo-physical properties, and defect-inducing phenomena, varying process parameters affect the likelihood of specific printing defects. Thus, printability maps serve as valuable tools to identify defect-prone process parameter combinations, delineate at-risk regions, and guide the selection of optimal conditions to enhance AM design (see Fig. 1). These maps incorporate the maximum hatch spacing (Equation (13) in Table 7), which the melt pool geometry determines to ensure sufficient overlap between tracks in multi-scan prints. In this work, however, we focus solely on single-track scenarios, even though prior studies have shown that single-track printability maps can effectively identify optimal processing windows for fabricating defect-free 3D coupons and more complex testing specimens.
